stem: A 72-year-old patient presents with fatigue and pallor. Laboratory tests reveal iron deficiency anemia. He reports no overt gastrointestinal bleeding. Considering the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in elderly patients, which of the following is the most likely source?
stemHtml: A 72-year-old patient presents with fatigue and pallor. Laboratory tests reveal iron deficiency anemia. He reports no overt gastrointestinal bleeding. Considering the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in elderly patients, which of the following is the most likely source? (Question Id: 501022)
keywords: “72-year-old / elderly patient” – Age is the strongest clue; iron deficiency anemia in elderly is most often due to colon carcinoma.
“Iron deficiency anemia” – Confirms the type of anemia and points to chronic blood loss, usually gastrointestinal in the elderly.
keywordsHtml:
1. “72-year-old / elderly patient” – Age is the strongest clue; iron deficiency anemia in elderly is most often due to colon carcinoma.
  2. “Iron deficiency anemia” – Confirms the type of anemia and points to chronic blood loss, usually gastrointestinal in the elderly.

E.title: Colon carcinoma
E.body:
Colon carcinoma (colorectal cancer) is the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in elderly men and postmenopausal women in developed countries, even in the absence of obvious bleeding.
The tumor can cause occult (hidden) blood loss into the stool due to chronic, low-grade mucosal erosion or ulceration. This slow, persistent blood loss over time can deplete the body's iron stores and lead to anemia.
Because the blood loss is not visible, the anemia is often the first presenting symptom, necessitating a thorough workup including colonoscopy to rule out malignancy.
Colon cancer incidence increases with age, making it a top differential in elderly patients presenting with unexplained anemia.
E.bodyHtml:
• Colon carcinoma (colorectal cancer) is the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in elderly men and postmenopausal women in developed countries, even in the absence of obvious bleeding.
  • The tumor can cause occult (hidden) blood loss into the stool due to chronic, low-grade mucosal erosion or ulceration. This slow, persistent blood loss over time can deplete the body's iron stores and lead to anemia.
  • Because the blood loss is not visible, the anemia is often the first presenting symptom, necessitating a thorough workup including colonoscopy to rule out malignancy.
  • Colon cancer incidence increases with age, making it a top differential in elderly patients presenting with unexplained anemia.

A.title: Duodenal ulcer
A.body:
Duodenal ulcers can cause chronic blood loss and iron deficiency anemia, but they are more commonly associated with younger adults.
Usually presents with epigastric pain or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, which this patient does not report.
A.bodyHtml:
• Duodenal ulcers can cause chronic blood loss and iron deficiency anemia, but they are more commonly associated with younger adults.
  • Usually presents with epigastric pain or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, which this patient does not report.

B.title: Crohn’s disease
B.body:
Crohn’s disease can cause malabsorption and anemia, but its typical onset is younger (20–40 years).
Chronic blood loss is usually mild, and other symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, or weight loss are common.
B.bodyHtml:
• Crohn’s disease can cause malabsorption and anemia, but its typical onset is younger (20–40 years).
  • Chronic blood loss is usually mild, and other symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, or weight loss are common.

C.title: Celiac disease
C.body:
Celiac disease can cause iron deficiency anemia due to malabsorption, but it usually presents earlier in life.
Less common as a new diagnosis in the elderly.
C.bodyHtml:
• Celiac disease can cause iron deficiency anemia due to malabsorption, but it usually presents earlier in life.
  • Less common as a new diagnosis in the elderly.

D.title: Gastric bypass
D.body:
Can lead to iron deficiency due to reduced absorption in the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
Relevant only if there is a history of bariatric surgery, which is not mentioned here.
D.bodyHtml:
• Can lead to iron deficiency due to reduced absorption in the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
  • Relevant only if there is a history of bariatric surgery, which is not mentioned here.

keyConcept: In elderly patients, iron deficiency anemia is most often due to occult gastrointestinal bleeding, commonly from colon carcinoma. Evaluation should include colonoscopy to rule out malignancy, even in the absence of visible blood.

diagrams.description: This diagram illustrates a stepwise clinical approach to evaluating iron deficiency anemia in elderly patients, emphasizing occult gastrointestinal blood loss as the primary cause. It highlights key pathways including initial laboratory confirmation, followed by targeted investigations such as colonoscopy to identify sources like colon carcinoma, along with other potential causes such as angiodysplasia and peptic ulcer disease.
